title: Using a solar wax melter
subtitle: Old comb, cappings, and burr wax all yield clean beeswax in a solar melter. No electricity, no supervision.
excerpt: A solar wax melter uses direct sunlight to melt beeswax out of old comb, washings, and cappings, allowing the wax to run through a filter into a collection tray while the debris stays behind. On a good summer day a single load of cappings gives a block of clean wax within an hour. Here is how to set up the melter, manage the output, and filter it for clean blocks.
sourceNotes: NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), wax processing section. Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), Internet Archive, chapter on wax extraction. BBKA technical notes on comb and wax management. British Beeswax standards for processed wax.

glossaryTerms.definition: The thin layer of beeswax sealing each cell of capped honey. Removed during extraction by slicing or scratching off the surface. The lightest, cleanest wax in the hive.
The dark, granular residue left in the solar melter or wax press after the wax has been extracted. Contains pollen, propolis, cocoon fibres, and debris. Not useable as wax.

content.text: A solar wax melter is a box with a glass lid that sits facing the sun. Old frames,
cappings

, and burr wax placed inside the box reach 60-70°C in direct summer sun, well above the melting point of beeswax at 62-65°C. The liquid wax runs through a mesh filter into a tray at the bottom. When it cools, it lifts out as a block.
What to put in the melter
Honey cappings from extraction, the lightest, highest-yield material.
Old dark brood comb that has been retired from the hive. Very old brood comb has a low wax yield due to cocoon buildup but is still worth processing.
Burr wax and brace comb scraped from the hive during inspections.
Wax moth-damaged frames. The wax moth itself does not damage the wax, only the comb structure, so melting wax-moth frames still gives useable wax.
Setting up for a session
Position the melter on a level surface angled toward the sun at 45-60°. South-facing in the UK works from late morning through mid-afternoon.
Line the collection tray with an old cotton cloth or a double layer of gauze as a secondary filter. The built-in mesh removes the largest debris but not fine propolis.
Load cappings or broken comb into the upper chamber. Do not overload, a packed-tight load melts slower and overflows into the
slum gum
channel rather than through the filter.
Close the glass lid and leave for 1-3 hours. The wax runs through and collects in the lower tray.
Collecting the wax block

Allow the wax to cool completely in the tray before removing it. Warm wax bends and cracks when peeled out. Once cold, the block lifts free and can be stored as is or remelted through a finer cotton filter for cosmetic or craft use.
The slum gum remaining in the upper chamber can be composted. Do not put it in a hive, the propolis in it is attractive to wax moths.
On cloudy days

A solar melter needs sustained direct sun. A partly cloudy UK afternoon may not get the load hot enough to melt fully, the wax softens but stays solid. Save the melting sessions for clear summer days, and store wax material in a cool dry space between sessions. Cappings stored in a bucket wait well for a sunny fortnight.
